@abbyad @browndav I still think we need to decide if we want to save the form if it's invalid (fails validation or is not complete).  If we save the form and respond with an error message to resend then we will have duplicates, which would need to be resolved on Kujua by the admin.  If we reject invalid forms and ask to be completed again, we could potentially lose data or cause grief for the reporter.  We should probably go with one for now.  At this point my suggestion is to have not-too-harsh validation rules and only accept messages/forms that are valid.

1) My error code was specifically to distinguish identical messages. I agree that it looks better without error codes, so I am torn on that because a CHW reports it an error string to their supervisor it may be a case of broken telephone by the time an admin hears about it. That said, the error message is logged in Kujua as a sent message so may not be an issue. Lets stay without error codes.

2) As for whether or not to save the messages, can we have the default to download only those that pass validation? It could be an advanced option to view messages that failed validation.

3a) I like it that you are including the form name in the error message. The error messages I wrote were close to 160 chars so we would need to work that out better to avoid sending response as multiple messages. We could use the form's short name (which should be less than 14 chars) but regardless using the first X chars of name, replacing cut off section with '...'.

3b) Would be easier to read with quotes around form name in the message.

Bump. It'd be great if we could do a couple of additional things here:

First, we should really test the full receive pipeline. Ideally, this would involve us sending a valid Textforms-formatted message to an SMSSync instance, and ensuring that it shows up in Kujua.

Next, we should take a look at the error-handling path -- send a totally invalid Textforms message, or one with missing fields, and make sure that we correctly reject the message by auto-replying (via SMS) with a human-readable error message.

Once we can do these two things, I think we'd be okay to close this issue.

We're currently just planning to use Textforms as a human-writable message protocol. We _could_ support it in the serializer, but it'd probably just bloat the binary (and the SMS messages it generates) with minimal benefit.

The names, locations etc. of government facilities are typically in the public domain, so I wouldn't bother encrypting facility IDs unless/until we have a user story asking for it. Different matter for individual's IDs.

In CouchDB, yes. It's possible to write each row to the response individually in order to stream results back to the client. Use send('data') inside the while loop to do that. The only problem is that in the browser you can't read a streamed response using XHR so you always end up buffering it all in memory anyway. If this is a list function that will be rendered by the browser as well as the server then it's best avoided, if it's just a server-rendered list function then by all means use the send() function instead of accumulating all the rows in memory.

before closing this ticket let's take a minute to outline all the cases we need to support.  and also make sure we have some tests around them.

_1) Valid message test_
Parse/accept valid (required fields exist) textforms message, assert fields on record are created, assert empty .errors, assert positive response is sent. **(done)**

_2) Invalid message test_
Parse/accept invalid (required field is missing) textforms message, assert fields on record are created, assert .errors contains appropriate error objects, assert response is sent with missing fields message. **(done)**

_3) Invalid message sent with missing fields fixed later_
Do invalid message test then send another message with fields fixed
Assert fields on _same_ record are updated
Assert the relevant error objs are cleared from .errors
This test requires a `data_record_merge` field defined on the form **(done)**

_4) Valid message sent with missing fields broken later_
Do valid message test
Assert fields on _same_ record are updated
Assert the relevant error objs are added to .errors
Assert we send a  response message with missing fields message
This test requires a `data_record_merge` field defined on the form **(done)**

Hi @endor,

Answers ahead. I might break this in to a couple posts.

Answer one:

We should probably defer handling of the "localized strings" -- e.g. { en: "foo", de: "foo" } -- to a locale function that, when given a list of preferred locales (ordered by preference), knows how to extract and return the correct string. There may be a huge number of languages later on, so the `foo.en || foo.fr` approach won't scale. Something like:

``` javascript
  var convert = fuunction (_json, _locales) {
    ...
    var string = extract_locale(string_or_object, _locales);
    ...
  }
```

Answer two and three:

Let's use the labels and types provided by the JSON. The muvuku-generated JSON is intended to be a one-time extraction, to get our form definitions out of the legacy muvuku-data.c format and in to something more manageable. We can _definitely_ adjust the JSON form definitions after the fact -- especially if it lets us avoid testing the `validate` keys directly and/or simplifies the `convert` function.

Special characters:

I made a mistake in the legacy-to-json converter, and missed translation of `\11` from the GSM alphabet to UTF-8. I'll check in a fix, and update the .json file. It looks like only the PSI Cameroon file has that problem.

Answer four:

Currently, all fields in Muvuku are effectively optional, because the SIM application allows CHWs to submit incomplete forms (e.g. to avoid data loss when signal or power loss is imminent). We have support for on-handset storage in the Muvuku dev version, which means we can remove the okay-to-send-incomplete-forms thing, and actually start requiring fields.

I think this is another case where we'll want to manually change the JSON after our final legacy-to-json export. Can we have `convert` check for a `required` attribute and -- if it's undefined, is false, or is null -- assume that the field is _not_ required?

Answer five:

Can we do something similar to what we're doing in item four, above? Specifically, let's assume there should be a `title` attribute in the JSON (pick a good place and key for it), and drop back to some kind of sane default if it's not present.

Just like in the other cases, we can manually add them to the JSON files after our final export.

```
http://dev.medicmobile.org:5984/kujua-base/_design/kujua-base/_rewrite/VPD/data_records.csv?startkey=%5B%220b55865e94fee64a9f709cb10352f74f%22%2C%22VPD%22%2C%22Damak%22%2C%7B%7D%5D&endkey=%5B%220b55865e94fee64a9f709cb10352f74f%22%2C%22VPD%22%2C%22Damak%22%5D&form=VPD&include_docs=true&descending=true&dh_name=Damak
```

becomes:

```
http://dev.medicmobile.org:5984/kujua-base/_design/kujua-base/_rewrite/VPD/data_records.csv?include_docs=true
```

Note that the start/end keys are excluded so that the **new** data can be imported into Klipfolio. The side effect is that without the keys all forms in the db are exported and field columns become meaningless. Therefore you can only import data if your instance has only 1 form.

Essentially what would be useful is a URL for which we have the following params, default values in brackets:

**Necessary:**
- **form** [null] if null return the whole incoming message (structured or unstructured) in a column

*_Nice to have, highest priority at top: *_
- **facility_name** [null] if specified return only reports from that facility. include child facilities if return_child_facilities is true
- **return_child_facilities** [true]
- **include_forms** [false] relevant only if form=null
- **include_messages** [true] relevant only if form=null
- **start_date** [1970]
- **end_date** [2099]
- **descending** [true]
- **include_docs** [true]
- **locale** [en]

The output fields would be similar to what they are now, I'd suggest we have the following:

```
date, sender number, sender name, sender facility, form fields... (or message contents if form=null)
```

Ok, here is how you can set things via query string. All params with a start _ are considered special, and anything else binds to a input for form values to prefill. So the _ params are:
- _hide_topbar - set to true so the dashboard topbar will not be displayed
- _locale - preset the local the form will render in
- _sync_url - set the sync_url value
- _gateway_num - set the gateway number
- _debug - show the debug panel
- _textforms_option - show the textforms checkbox option
- _use_textforms - if set to 'true' then toggle it to on. 

Any other value gets bound to the actual form input. For example: `test_strips_oos=2` will set the test_strips_oos to value 2.

Talked with Milan and Ryan and just wanted to clarify a couple of things.

For this issue, we're looking at letting the user select a particular facility from an autocomplete/drop-down list; we'll use that facility to determine which roles the user should have. For example, selecting "Dave's District" would make the user a district_admin (cascading all of the way down), selecting "Dave's Nation" would make the user a national_office_admin (cascading all of the way down), etc.

Those roles are enforced at the database level. However, they don't differentiate between particular districts, or between particular national offices -- they're based only on the "level".

The UI will use the facility selection to create a "soft" limitation -- the user will see only his/her own facility by default. However, this won't be enforced at the database level. A determined district_admin for "District A" could, using curl or another HTTP client, read/write data belonging to "District B".

There is a way to provide a "hard" limitation at the database level (i.e. instruct the database to disallow writes if a record's facility ID doesn't match the user's facility ID), but it involves manufacturing a role for each facility, and will likely require more effort.

I'm proposing that -- at least for now -- this issue _does not_ include the group generation "hard limit" I just wrote about in the previous paragraph.

After some discussion on IRC we came up with this strategy for first cut which basically adds a form mgmt screen with the following features:

Form upload process for json form definition which includes:
- Validate form code and json object validate on upload.  
- Enforce uniqueness constraint on form codes, compare with installed form codes, form codes in the system need to be unique so one form doesn't overwrite another.
- ability to change form code during upload process to adjust form code if not unique
- form code string should validate with `[\w]+` (1 or more word characters)
- no immediate support for form versioning

List of installed forms with ability to delete or download installed form as nicely formatted JSON file.  Use case is to download an existing form, modify it in a text editor and then upload as a new form.  Several iterations of adding a new form and deleting old forms would allow you to test your system.

Change current set of forms that are shipped with KL build.  Only ship example forms in new builds.  The example forms may or may not be delete-able (not that important).  Main thing is to allow for new JSON form definition uploads.

New forms will get saved somewhere in ddoc.app_settings structure so that they persist on app updates.  Likely maintaining the same structure as ddoc.views.lib.jsonforms which allows form lookup by key/form code.

JSON-Schema/json-edit validation possibly in the future.

There is a potential problem scenario where we start accepting bad data.  Admin starts by creating form ABC and deploying it, people are submitting ABC normally, then admin decides to delete ABC and upload a new ABC with different fields; now we are getting bad data.  For now our answer is "mess with your forms at your peril" or "get it right before you start collecting data".  We need to make the admin user aware of this potential situation. The alternative/fix might be to keep all history of form creation available to the backend so we can check deleted or inactive forms and make sure there are no form code conflicts.

I believe Marc (perhaps with my help; I can't remember to be honest) added this; 'month' is just intended to be a shortcut for a 'select' field with choices [ [1, "January"], ..., [12, "December"] ](properly localized, if necessary).

There are two reasons for this, and one of them is much better than the other:

  (1) Reduces duplication inside of a JSON form when collecting lots of month-related data (e.g. on several forms), and

  (2) The muvuku compiler doesn't (yet) know how to de-duplicate select lists; using the 'month' type causes Muvuku to use a built-in month list, and thus only store a single copy in the binary. This reduces code size, and lets us fit more forms/questions within the ~30KB we have on a parallel SIM.

Is this referring to sub strings in the message, or in the phone number?
Seems like this is done?

Both, I think. In general, most databases build prefix indexes; some databases will let you talk them in to indexing the result of a function (Couch included, in the map step), but in general the number of index entries you'd have to generate would blow up according to (n^2 + n) / 2 -- still O(n^2) per-item; prohibitive in terms of both time and space.

You're left with linear searches, ideally over a subset of the database. There's a couchdb-lucene setting to allow this, but we'll need to be careful with it. Best to _not_ do these kind of linear searches from the client side in javascript.

Splitting the phone number in to chunks and using prefix matching over those chunks is a great idea as it's still O(1) per item. We could probably adapt this strategy to structured SMSs as well, and then we'd avoid the need to use couchdb-lucene's linear-time substring matching option.

Dave

Just some quick terminology background, from the manual and elsewhere: "In DHIS 2 there are three dimensions that describe the aggregated data being collected and stored in the database; the where (organizational unit), the what (data element), and the when (period) [a timestamp]". [There's also a data "value", which is the actual usually-numeric value]. Effectively, an "indicator" (the unit of record for DHIS2) says something like "At Nairobi hospital, we had 100 bathtubs full of morphine as of 10:00am on 4/1/2013". In the database, the "organizational unit" and "data element" for any imported value are identifiers that look like `gP6hn503KUX`; these IDs refer to an existing organizationalUnit or dataElement that's been registered with the DHIS2 system. The DHIS2 system has a dictionary of these, so elsewhere there might be an organizationalUnit record that looks like `[ 'gP6hn503KUX', 'organizationalUnit', 'Nairobi Hospital' ]`.

Highlighting this:

```
We can currently filter messages by specifying url params for start and end date, which filter
based on the Reported Date. This works to reduce the size, but the CSV output does not contain
what a user would expect. Scheduled messages always have a Reported Date based on the report
that generated them, regardless of when the scheduled message actually goes out. For example,
filtering for messages in March will yield those scheduled in March, even if they are only going
to be sent in July. Conversely, it will omit many of the messages actually sent in March since
they are likely associated to a reported date from a previous month.
```

### Requirements
1. We need to be able to return only messages sent within a given timeframe
2. This only applies to message download, not to form and audit downloads
3. By default we will return all messages

### Nice to haves
1. Filtering by any column
2. User friendly durations in date filters, eg: "3 months", interpreted as "between 3 months ago and now"

### Proposal

```
/export/messages?state=sent,pending&stateFrom=20140201&stateTo=20140301
```

Any messages which entered one of the `state`s between the `stateFrom` and `stateTo` dates will be returned.

Essentially we need to get the following for analytics:

"who missed an appointment in last X days" ==> filter on Pending Timestamp between start & end date.
"who has upcoming appointment next X days" ==> filter on Scheduled Timestamp between start & end date.

Since these visualizations will be on a rolling time we will provide delta times.

Here is an example:
`/export/message?filter='Pending Timestamp'&filterFrom=-14&filterTo=+30` to get all messages with a Pending Timestamp value between 14 days ago and 30 days from now.

Example:

```
/export/messages?startkey=%5B9999999999999%2C%7B%7D%5D&endkey=%5B0%5D&tz=-720&reduce=false&filter_state=scheduled&filter_state_from=0&filter_state_to=10
```

So the parameters are:
- `filter_state`: The key for the state. Valid values are: 'received', 'scheduled', 'pending', 'sent', 'cleared', 'muted'
- `filter_state_from`: The number of days to add to the current date to define the minimum. Can be negative. The minimum is rounded down to the start of the day.
- `filter_state_to`: The number of days to add to the current date to define the maximum. Can be negative. The maximum is rounded up to the end of the day.

It is important to note that messages returned may be in a state other than the filter_state value, for example, requesting `scheduled` messages will return messages that were scheduled to be sent within the filter window, but may have since been `sent`.

Just a reminder; Muvuku for parallel SIMs doesn't support UCS-2 or UTF-8 form codes. We also can't (yet) send UCS-2 data in text fields collected by Muvuku, because it cuts the maximum amount of collectable data by more than half -- every field, every delimiter, every header takes twice as much space because the encoding of a single SMS is all-or-nothing.

With respect to Kujua and the muvuku webapp, though, everything should just work. Javascript uses either UCS-2 or UTF-16 internally to represent strings (most engines use UTF-16), and `JSON.parse` should work with UTF-8 encodings out of the box as long as they're representable by that UTF-16 or UCS-2 internal encoding. IIRC, UTF-16 can represent any Unicode codepoint (the top half of Unicode is represented using "surrogate pairs"), while UCS-2 can only represent the bottom half of Unicode (which still usually suffices for any pronounceable human language). In any case, the Nepali alphabet is located at around 2,300 decimal, which means it should... in theory... just work.

Actually, I take that back, there's an important exception: some "characters" are made up of multiple "code units", i.e. keystrokes compine to form a single glyph visually, but they still (in Javascript) count as separate characters: http://es5.github.io/x6.html#x6.

Code that accesses strings character-by-character -- or, say, pulls out the first four characters of a string -- might visually appear to only contain an incomplete prefix of the original string.

Yeah, here are a couple examples from the form of that last exception:

```
> "सुरु ".length
< 5
> "बन्द".length
< 4
```

Closing, was mainly due to couchdb-lucene 0.9.0 not supporting POST.  Opening new issues for additional lucene limitations.

1) Split the patient IDs array and perform multiple queries and combine the data. We'd end up doing more queries on large installs which will be slower, but again, we can solve performance later (eg: generating daily data and caching if we have to).
2) Rewrite everything to use views rather than lucene. This is the proper approach but I think couchdb views are too restricted to accomplish it (which is why I went for lucene in the first place). The problem is when you have to combine data between documents, for example: find all Visit reports for patients that don't have a Delivery report. As map/reduce handles one document at a time I can't see a way to accomplish this.
3) Denormalise the statistics. For example, write a sentinel transform which updates a number_of_visits field on the Registration when a Visit is received. If we denormalise all the data we need for analytics it'll be lightning fast, and simple to query, however as with all denormalisations it's possible for the data to get out of sync with reality (eg: if you delete a Visit, do we decrement the counter in the Registration?)
4) Perform one unlimited lucene/view query to get all required data into node, and then iterate over the data to generate the statistics. This may require too much memory to be practical.
We chose option 1 as the low risk option.
+1 for option 1 – thanks for the thoughtful analysis.

Just a note on option three: the eventual-consistency / lack of atomic update operations in CouchDB would make that even harder, and the consistency would definitely break if a replication operation was attempted.

All the tricks I tried with regards to injection resulted in invalid syntax. With SQL you usually terminate the injection with `--` to comment out the rest of the query, but I don't think there is a comment operator in Lucene. This means whatever the user enters the query ends with `AND district:xyz` which cannot be shortcircuited with a disjunction or ignored with a comment.

Escaping the query while being the safest approach would really reduce the power of the solution. For example, ANC Analytics is using the lucene syntax to show all reports for `patient_id:xyz`.

I worry that if we attempted to write our own syntax it would end up trying to reproduce much of the functionality of the Lucene syntax and we'd be no better off.

I'll detect syntax errors and change the error message to have a link to our help page on query syntax for now, and we can reevaluate if users find the syntax difficult or injection is found to be possible.

@garethbowen  and I decided to:

Only have one changes listener and process all changes on one document and send one update after all transitions have been applied. Reducing amount of changes feed subscriptions reduces latency in processing a change.  We estimate a large gain here because currently each change on a document will trigger all the transitions.  As is, a document that needs 3 updates to be applied will trigger 24 changes if you have 8 transitions.  This would be reduced to one change event and one update event for N transitions, not sure what big O notation would be here but it significantly improves the algorithm.

Something to complicate this a bit. It's not specifically related to a filter change, but it's at least somewhat related.

If the user creates a new contact while all contacts in the left pane are hidden by a filter, it's not entirely clear what the right behavior is – we want the user to see that a new contact was created, we want the user to be able to edit the contact, but we also want to maintain some semblance of filter consistency in the left pane. We probably also want to avoid just clearing the filters, since that could cause a pretty dramatic UI shift and possibly confuse people. IIRC, we're currently showing the new contact in the right pane (regardless of whether it shows up in the left pane).

If we clear the right pane only on a filter change, I think it's probably fine. If we clear the right pane whenever the item in the left pane vanishes, I think we'd bump up against the new-contact UI problem.

We talked about this in Slack already, but I wanted to make sure it made it in here. This seems like a logical place for a discussion at least, and we can split it off if it becomes clear that they're separate issues.
